analysis.one_liner: Extends full child labor protections, now denied on farms, to children working in agriculture.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have given farmworker children the same child labor protections as other children, was referred to the Senate health committee in May 2001 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal child labor law treats farm work differently from every other job: children as young as 12 can legally work unlimited hours in the fields outside school, and 16-year-olds can do hazardous work that would be illegal in a factory. The CARE Act would have ended that two-tier system — applying the same minimum ages to agriculture as to other industries, raising the hazardous-work age to 18, and stiffening fines and penalties for employers who violate child labor rules. It also required employers to report injuries to workers under 18, and directed the Labor Department to collect real data on where and how children are working illegally. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers working in American agriculture — the sons and daughters of farmworkers, many in migrant families — gain the same protection from overwork and hazardous jobs that children in every other industry already have. Those injured on the job would gain a new right to sue their employer and higher fines would deter violations. Communities near large farms gain better data, since the bill requires employers to report every injury to a worker under 18 and the Labor Department to publish a biennial report on child labor and its hazards. Family farms that want their own children to help are explicitly carved out and may keep doing so.

how_it_helps.text: It applies the Fair Labor Standards Act's standard child labor age limits to farm work, so children under roughly 14 could no longer legally be employed in commercial agriculture, and 14- and 15-year-olds could no longer work unrestricted hours in fields, as they can today [S2][S3].
It raises from 16 to 18 the minimum age for doing hazardous farm work such as operating heavy machinery or handling dangerous chemicals, a floor other industries have long had at 18 [S2][S3].

It raises civil fines for child labor violations from a $10,000 maximum to $500–$15,000 and adds up to 5 years in prison for willful or repeat violations that kill or permanently disable a child worker, plus a new right for injured children or their families to sue the employer directly [S3].

It requires employers to report injuries and illnesses of workers under 18 to state agencies, and directs the Labor Department to compile biennial data on where and how minors are employed illegally — creating the first reliable national picture of farmwork injuries to children [S2][S3].
It preserves the family-farm tradition: children may still work for a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, or legal guardian on that relative's own farm outside school hours [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Agricultural employers — commercial farms and agribusiness — bear the cost: they could no longer hire children under 14 or work 16-year-olds in hazardous jobs, fines for violations rise from $10,000 to $15,000, and they face new reporting duties and lawsuits from injured children. Some low-income farm families also lose a source of income, since their teenage children could no longer work the long hours in the fields that currently supplement family wages.

drawbacks.text: Agricultural employers would face higher compliance costs and steeper penalties — civil fines rising from up to $10,000 to at least $500 and up to $15,000, new federal lawsuits for injuries or deaths, and possible criminal liability — with no offsetting support, a burden small family operations could feel most heavily [S3].

Some low-income farm families rely on their children's agricultural earnings, and restricting when and how many hours minors may work removes that income, which is why the bill kept a narrow exemption only for children working for a parent or grandparent on that relative's own farm [S2][S3].

The bill adds significant reporting and paperwork: every employer of a minor must report any injury or illness that costs work time to the state employment security agency, including details of the job, the circumstances, and the treating physician's report — a real administrative load for the many small farms that employ teenage workers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are substantial for the estimated hundreds of thousands of children who work in American agriculture: the same age minimums and hazardous-work rules as other workers, larger fines, new injury reporting, and better data — all at little cost to the federal budget, since the bill simply authorizes necessary appropriations and relies on existing Labor Department machinery [S2][S3]. The costs fall almost entirely on agricultural employers, who would lose the ability to hire younger children for longer hours and face up to $15,000 in penalties per violation, and on some low-income farm families who currently rely on children's earnings [S3]. Congress has since noted that children employed in agriculture can still legally be far younger and working far longer hours than other child workers, so the bill's aim remains a live gap in the law — but this 2001 version never advanced far enough for the objections of farm employers and grower-state members to be heard or resolved.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate's labor committee in May 2001, and with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote, it simply expired when that Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin (D-IA) introduced the Children's Act for Responsible Employment of 2001 on May 10, 2001 [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it the same day to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee — its only action beyond introduction [S5].
The bill never received a committee hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or any further action; the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 without moving it [S1][S5].
It drew five cosponsors, all Senate Democrats, and no Republican support was recorded [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agricultural employers keep the exemptions that let them hire children at younger ages, for longer hours, and in hazardous jobs than any other industry permits, with the same penalty ceilings; the children working in those fields gained nothing.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for nearly two years without a hearing, markup, or vote, letting it expire at the end of the 107th Congress [S5].

against.name: Agricultural employer interests (growers and agribusiness)
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending standard child labor rules and penalties to agricultural hiring, an industry position widely reported in the long-running debate over farmworker child labor; no such activity appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored and cosponsored only by Democrats (the sponsor plus 5 of 49 Senate Democrats), and it never advanced far enough for a recorded vote to show whether Republicans opposed it or simply never considered it [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill repeals the special child labor exemptions that let agriculture hire children at younger ages and in more dangerous conditions than other employers, raises fines to $15,000, adds injury-reporting duties, and lets injured children sue — a direct compliance cost to farms and agribusiness. Its defeat preserved the status quo, under which farmwork remains the least-protected setting for working children.

Family farms keep an explicit exemption letting their own children, grandchildren, nieces and nephews work on the family's farm outside school hours, but larger family operations that hire outside minors would face the same fines and reporting rules as commercial growers. For ordinary consumers the effect is negligible; for farmworker children it is the difference between the protections other workers' children get and none at all.

industries.industry: Labor Department and state labor enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill authorizes funding, formalizes coordination with state and local agencies and nonprofits, and requires states to share injury and death data with the Labor Department, expanding its enforcement reach. That added capacity exists to protect child workers, so the industry's interest here runs alongside the public's.
